findings.title: Email lookup is case-sensitive, allowing blocked emails to bypass the block
findings.body: `should_block?` performs a case-sensitive lookup with `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`. Email addresses are case-insensitive per RFC 5321. If an admin blocks "Spam@Example.com", a user signing up with "spam@example.com" will not be blocked. The email should be normalized (e.g., downcased) both when storing and when looking up, similar to how `User` uses `Email.downcase` elsewhere in the codebase.

findings.title: should_block? has side effects during validation, corrupting match statistics
findings.body: `should_block?` increments `match_count` and sets `last_match_at` as a side effect. This method is called from `EmailValidator#validate_each`, which runs during `user.valid?`. If the user record subsequently fails to save for an unrelated reason (e.g., username taken), the match_count is still incremented. This means match_count reflects validation attempts rather than actual blocked registrations, making the statistics unreliable.

findings.title: record.save can fail silently, losing statistics without indication
findings.body: In `should_block?`, `record.save` is called without checking its return value or using `save!`. If the save fails (e.g., due to the uniqueness validation triggering a race condition, or a database error), the match_count increment and last_match_at update are silently lost. The method still returns the block decision based on the in-memory object, hiding the failure. Consider using `update_columns` to bypass validations for this statistics update, or at minimum checking the return value.

findings.title: BlockedEmail.should_block? is called even when value is nil or blank
findings.body: `validate_each` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` without first checking if `value` is present. If `value` is nil (e.g., during an intermediate validation state), this will execute a database query with `where(email: nil)` and attempt to call `match_count += 1` on a nil record (which is safe due to the `if record` guard), but it still issues a pointless database query on every validation of a record with a nil email. A guard clause like `return if value.blank?` at the top would be more robust.

findings.title: Domain setting is insufficiently escaped before use in regex, allowing regex injection
findings.body: `email_in_restriction_setting?` only escapes dots via `gsub('.', '\.')` before interpolating the admin-provided setting into `Regexp.new`. If the setting contains other regex metacharacters (e.g., `(`, `)`, `+`, `*`, `[`), they will be interpreted as regex syntax. A malicious or mistaken admin input could cause a `RegexpError` crash or unintended matching behavior. Use `Regexp.escape` on each domain segment, or at minimum document that `|` is the only expected special character and validate the input format.

findings.title: should_block? issues a full save with validations just to update statistics
findings.body: Calling `record.save` triggers the full ActiveRecord lifecycle including `before_validation :set_defaults` and the `validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true` checks. The uniqueness validation issues an additional SELECT query. Since the record already exists and we're only updating counters, `record.update_columns(match_count: record.match_count, last_match_at: Time.zone.now)` would be more efficient and avoid the unnecessary validation overhead on every blocked-email check.
